title: 3-Read Friday #9: Maths Gems, the Hawthorne Effect, and Fun Lessons
author: Barton, Craig
summary: Issue nine leans toward the culture and practice of teaching over pure pedagogy. Barton opens with Jo Morgan's 172nd "5 Maths Gems" round-up, calling her series his "all-time favourite" and singling out Nathan Day's "snake" task structure and Hannah Smithe's "speak like a scholar" resources. He then covers InnerDrive's piece on the Hawthorne Effect and teacher wait times during observations, zeroing in on "action bias" — the tendency of observed teachers to rush explanations and cut wait time simply because they feel they should be "doing something." He closes with Thahmina Begum's advice for handling the end-of-term "can we have a fun lesson today?" question, agreeing with her closing point that "learning is not the antithesis of fun." Two of the three items concern how teachers behave under observation and classroom-culture pressure, tipping this issue toward Practice & Culture.
points: Barton calls out action bias — teachers doing something rather than nothing when observed — as the mechanism by which classroom observation quietly degrades wait time and explanation quality.
He treats Morgan's "5 Maths Gems" as a recurring highlight of the newsletter, specifically naming Day's snake tasks and Smithe's "speak like a scholar" resources as standouts.
He endorses Begum's final point verbatim as the most important takeaway of her piece: that learning and fun are not opposites.
quotes: Jo’s Maths Gems are my all-time favourite series of blog posts. Every few weeks, she scours the Internet to pick out the best ideas, resources and pedagogies shared by maths teachers.
I see this all the time when coaching and supporting teachers: when being watched, teachers feel the need to do something rather than nothing.
As a result, they end up doing things that might not be in students’ best interests, like reducing wait times, rushing explanations, or simply failing to shut up and just letting students crack on.
Well, Thahmina has some great suggestions (and some things to avoid!) in this post.
I think the point made in the final section is the most important: learning is not the antithesis of fun
